# PLAN
## OF THIS WORK.

Just as the history of the French monarchy is the collection and the examination of what our predecessors have taught us concerning the origin and the progress of that monarchy; so the *History of the Heavens* <note>original: "l'Hiſtoire du Ciel"</note> is the collection and the discussion of what those before us have thought or learned from their ancestors regarding the origin of the heavens, and its relationship with the earth.

A wise historian does not include within the main body of his Work all the records <term>mémoires: here referring to historical accounts, notes, or primary source documents</term> that he may have been able to gather. He makes a selection.

<summary>The author defines the "History of the Heavens" by comparing it to political history, explaining that it is a curated examination of ancestral knowledge regarding the cosmos and its link to Earth.</summary>
<keywords>French monarchy, History of the Heavens, historiography, origins of the universe, methodology, historical records</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---

# PLAN

Everything that is found to be frivolous or clearly contrary to known facts; everything that is put forward without caution or lacks plausibility, he <note>The author is referring back to the "wise historian" mentioned on the previous page.</note> rejects, and makes use only of that which can naturally be linked together, be made palatable <note>original: "se faire goûter", implying that the information is presented in a way that is satisfying and acceptable to the reader's reason</note>, and form a coherent sequence. 

In undertaking, therefore, the history of the formation of the heavens and the origin, whether of the different names given to the celestial bodies <term>corps célestes: planets, stars, and other objects in space</term>, or of the influences attributed to them; our primary concern is to employ only what the most rational minds or the peoples best informed of the past have thought on the matter, and to set aside the bizarre opinions of many nations on this subject. We shall not go about collecting what is imagined by the Caribs, nor the Greenlanders, or other Savages <term>Sauvages: a historical term used by 18th-century French authors to describe indigenous peoples living in a state of nature; it reflects the Eurocentric biases of the Enlightenment era</term>, whom a...

<meta>catchword: a</meta>

<summary>The author explains his rigorous selection process for the "History of the Heavens," stating he will only include rational accounts from well-informed civilizations while excluding the mythologies of indigenous peoples.</summary>
<keywords>methodology, historiography, celestial bodies, Caribs, Greenlanders, Enlightenment, rationalism, cosmological origins</keywords>

This entire history will therefore be divided into four Books, which I shall name *The Poetic Heaven*, *The World of the Philosophers*, *The Physics of Moses*, and *The Consequences of the History of the Heavens*.

<margin>Subject of the first book.</margin>
The first may be titled *The Poetic Heaven*, because therein we shall seek the origin of the names that were given to the stars and planets in the most remote antiquity; as well as the progress of the monstrous worship and the fatal errors <note>The author refers here to the rise of paganism and astrology, which he views as "errors" resulting from the misuse of astronomical names.</note> with which the use of these names filled the world.

<margin>Regarding the second book.</margin>
The second book is titled *The World of the Philosophers*, because after the presentation of their most famous opinions on the origin of the heavens and the alleged influences the earth receives from them, we show not only what gave rise to the false ideas of either Epicurus <note>Epicurus: An ancient Greek philosopher who taught that the universe formed through the random motion of atoms, a view the author considers "imaginary."</note> or Descartes <note>Descartes: René Descartes, the famous French philosopher who proposed a mechanical "vortex" theory to explain the heavens, which was widely debated in the 18th century.</note>, and all other imaginary constructions; but also how much they are contrary to the truth and to the structure of the real world.

<margin>Of the fourth book.</margin>
The result of this comparison between sacred Physics and profane <note>Profane: Meaning secular, or knowledge derived from human reasoning rather than from sacred scripture.</note> Physics is to understand more precisely the limits of human science, and to bring it back to its proper scale, as well as to its true object. ### APPROBATION.

I have read, by order of My Lord the Chancellor <term>Chancellor: The head of the French judiciary who oversaw the licensing and censorship of all books published in the kingdom.</term>, a manuscript entitled *History of the Heavens considered according to the ideas of Poets, Philosophers, and Moses, etc.* by Mr. Pluche. One cannot give too much praise to the Author, who has directed all his aims toward religion and good morals. The Public has already applauded the first works to come from the same hand <note>This refers to Pluche's immensely popular previous work, "Spectacle de la Nature."</note>, and I do not doubt that they will again favorably receive this one, which offers a new system concerning Mythology, the whole of Pagan religion, and the use of reason—a system sustained with great erudition. At Paris, June 6, 1738.

### *On the origin of the names that antiquity has given to the various parts of the Heaven.*

We cannot judge soundly the origin of the names that antiquity has given to the various parts of the heaven and to all of nature, except insofar as we know what ideas occupied their minds, and what interests were able to move them. UNIVERSAL CUSTOMS.

### I.

### *The origin of the customs common to all Nations.*

One is sometimes astonished by the conformity found in several points between the practices of the people of God <note>The "people of God" refers to the ancient Israelites or Hebrews.</note> and those of nations surrendered to the crudest idolatry.

The Hebrews, like all other peoples, were in the habit of gathering to praise God in a distinguished and chosen location; of offering to God bread, salt, the fruits of the earth, and the ordinary elements of life, or of publicly thanking Him for them; of sacrificing victims; of eating in common that which had been offered to the Lord; and of joining songs and the sound of instruments to the act of thanksgiving.

It was also a common practice among the Hebrews and all peoples to bury the dead, to treat them with honor, and to gather near their tombs on certain days to praise God there. Subsequently, we will have occasion to note other equally universal customs.

<vocab>Hebrews, idolatry, sacrifices, funerary rites, religious conformity</vocab>

<summary>The author notes the surprising similarities in religious practices—such as communal worship, food offerings, and funeral rites—between the ancient Hebrews and pagan nations. He suggests these shared traditions point toward a common historical origin for all human customs.</summary>

To this end, the stars under which the sun was seen to pass and repass were divided into twelve equal portions*; because it had been observed that the sun traversed them once while the moon made its circuit approximately twelve times. Thus, the entire sequence of preparations and operations that were to occupy society over the course of an entire year was expressed by twelve words. And if the use of these twelve words and the twelve portions of the year corresponding to them has passed to most nations, it is further proof that it originates, as they all do, from the common source of the human race <note>A reference to the biblical idea that all humanity spread out from a single point (the plains of Shinar/Babel) after the Great Flood.</note>.

### VI.

*The Most Commonly Used Symbols. A Taste for Allegory.*

It was found beneficial to display a simple figure or a single letter in public to inform a large multitude all at once of the precise time when certain works were to begin in common, and of the time when certain festivals were to be celebrated. The use of this appeared so convenient that it was gradually extended, even to things other than the order of the calendar. Various symbols were devised to instruct the people in certain truths, or to recall them to mind by a certain resemblance between the figure and the thing intended to be understood.

This observation is important because it shows us what care was taken to preserve history, and by what means the tradition of great events was perpetuated. Fifty words were easy to remember, and fifty words of this sort were a very detailed history. From this comes the fact that the tenth chapter of Genesis alone, which simply places the names of Noah’s descendants end-to-end, contains a more extensive and a thousand times more satisfying erudition on the origin of nations than all of Greek and Roman literature, where the true origin of things is entirely disfigured and unrecognizable.

<margin>THE POETIC HEAVEN.</margin>perpetually before their eyes, let us first acquaint ourselves with the primary objects of their belief, their principal customs, and their most pressing needs.

Those descendants of Noah who settled in Egypt then held the same customs and the same religion as all other families. They worshipped the Creator. They gathered at the new moon to publicly glorify Him for His generosity and His admirable providence, which daily renews the provisions necessary for man. They ate together after prayers and offerings. They professed to await the resurrection of the body <note>original: "résurrection des corps"</note> and a better life where they would receive the reward for the justice they had practiced in this one. As a result of this conviction, the Egyptians treated dead bodies honorably, knowing they were destined by God to rise one day from the dust and pass into a completely different state. It is upon this that the respect for the dead is founded—a respect which, along with the sacrifice and the offering of bread and wine, spread from Chaldea <note>The region in southern Mesopotamia, considered by the author to be the "cradle of nations" following the Great Flood.</note> (that is to say, from the cradle of nations) generally into every country in the world. <margin>Circumstances peculiar to Egypt</margin>
But the particular layout of the land of the Egyptians, which the Nile floods every year toward the middle of summer, forced these people to take more precautions than were taken elsewhere to prevent the rapid destruction of their fathers' tombs. <margin>Signs and causes of the flood.</margin>
They noticed from year to year that the overflow was always preceded by an Etesian wind (*a*) which, blowing from the North to the South around the time of the sun's passage under the stars of the Crab <note>the zodiac sign Cancer</note>, pushed the vapors toward the South and gathered them in the heart of the country (*b*) from which the Nile originated. This caused abundant rains there, increased the river's water, and subsequently brought the flood into all of Egypt without a single drop of rain being felt there. Perhaps they did not conceive of this sequence of effects in the manner we have just represented. However, without reasoning uselessly on the causes and the production of the effect, they noticed that the blowing of the North wind was always followed by the inundation, and that the inundation was strong or weak according to the strength and duration of the wind, which were unequal from one year to the next. This wind, which had become the infallible sign of the rising waters, soon served as a rule for the inhabitants.

The convenience of these marks led to their multiplication; soon, all parts of the sky, the air, and the agricultural practices that interested them most—or which required fixed knowledge—were expressed through characters that shared a visible connection with them. Thoth <note>original: "Thotès ou Thot"</note>, one of the most ancient inhabitants of Egypt and perhaps the son of Ham <note>original: "Cham," the biblical son of Noah traditionally associated with the peopling of Africa</note>, or an Egyptian from the earliest times who was later given the name Thoth, devised a system of symbols that were easy to understand and remember. Such is the origin of the priestly order so ancient in Egypt, and whose principal function was always the study of the heavens and the inspection of the movements of the air. This residence, upon the structure of which much was refined over time, was then called simply and without any mystery the *labyrinth*, that is to say, the tower (*a*).

I will not tell you which winds were marked by the raven, by the ibis (which was a species of stork), by the Guinea fowl <note>original: "poule de Numidie"</note>, and by other birds that are seen so often in Egyptian monuments. The Dog Star or the rising of the star Sirius. <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, was crucial to Egyptian life as its "heliacal rising" (appearing just before sunrise) signaled the annual flooding of the Nile.</note>
</margin>
The second circumstance, and the one throughout the entire year upon which the Egyptian people had to keep the closest watch, was the rising of the star of the Nile. As soon as it freed itself from the sun's rays, or showed itself before dawn, it was certain that the sun was advancing under the sign of Leo, and that the flood would follow shortly. Since the warning provided by this star was their most important business, they formerly calculated the beginning of their year from its rising (*a*), and the entire sequence of their festivals. Instead, therefore, of depicting it in the form of a star—which would not have distinguished it from any other—they depicted it in a figure relating to its function and its name. They called it *the barker*, *the monitor*, *the dog-star*, *the gatekeeper*, or *the star that opens or closes one year and begins another*. When they wished to signify the renewal of the year, starting from the rising of the Dog Star, they depicted it in the form of a gatekeeper

<margin>The Poetic Heavens.</margin>recognizable by a key: or they even gave him two heads positioned back-to-back, one of an old man marking the expiring year, and the other of a young man marking the new year. <note>This description mirrors the Roman god Janus, though the author is linking these concepts to Egyptian celestial observations.</note> When it was necessary to warn the people of the moment to retreat as the flood approached, then instead of the two human-faced heads, a dog’s head was placed upon his shoulders. All these very simple and very intelligible notices were preceded by another equally necessary one, which was to indicate to the people the precise height they needed to give to the terraces to be surely above the strongest flood, without incurring useless expenses by raising them too high.

### X.

->*Symbols of the year. The solar year, Osiris.*<-

As all of society had an extreme need to regulate the order of its days, and to agree upon the times when it is necessary to assemble, rest, or work in common, symbolic writing was particularly useful in this regard, by the convenience of certain marks which, being displayed in public, announced festivals and labors in a simple and uniform manner.

# OF THE HEAVENS.

<margin>SYMBOLIC WRITING.</margin>
The progression of the year relates to three main subjects: 1st, the path of the sun; 2nd, the sequence of festivals for each season; and 3rd, the communal labors that must be performed. Let us begin with the symbols of the sun.

This celestial body, which—as the most magnificent object in nature—was so rightly chosen to represent the Almighty Being, also possessed its own character or mark in symbolic writing. This figure was related to the name given to it: it was called <term>Osiris</term> <note>Osiris was a central deity in ancient Egypt, often associated with the sun, the cycles of nature, and the afterlife.</note>. <margin>The governor or the sun.</margin> According to the most discerning and learned ancient authors <note>original: (a)</note>, this word signified the inspector, the charioteer or driver, the king, the guide, the moderator of the stars, the soul of the world, and the governor of nature. Based on the literal meaning of the terms from which it is composed, it signified *the government of the earth* <note>original: (b)</note>, which conveys the same meaning. It is because this name and this function were assigned—

---

<margin>(a) <note>original Latin: "Plutarch. de Isid. & Osirid. & Macrobe in somn. Scip. lib. 1. c. 20. The course of the year relates to three main objects: 1. the course of the sun; 2. the order of the festivals for each season; 3. the tasks that must be performed in common. Let us begin with the symbols of the sun.

<margin>SYMBOLIC WRITING.</margin>
This star, which—being the most magnificent object in nature—had been so justly chosen to be the symbol of the Almighty Being, also had its own character or mark in symbolic writing, and this figure was relative to the name given to it. # CONCERNING THE HEAVENS.

<margin>SYMBOLIC WRITING.</margin>

Let us come, then, to the symbol that properly regulated the sacred year—the order of the festivals.

### XI.

#### *The civil year. Isis.*

One could quite reasonably call the order of festivals here the "Ecclesiastical year"; since these festivals were religious assemblies where people made a profession of honoring God and glorifying Him for His providence. The investigation we are making into primitive customs and the meaning of ancient writing clearly concerns the times that preceded the introduction of idolatry <note>The author suggests a "pure" historical period where Egyptian symbols were merely tools for organization before they were worshipped as gods</note>. But since this order of days destined for work or for religious assemblies was the rule of society, we shall call it *the civil year*. It was hardly possible to designate the various festivals of the year more simply than by using the mark or symbol of the earth and its productions.

Her headdress was adorned with the horns of the ram, the bull, or the kids <note>Referring to the constellations of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini</note>, to mark the spring and its various stages. The harvest being completed in Egypt when the sun enters the Bull <note>The zodiac sign of Taurus</note>, the horns of the heifer were the sign of the great festival celebrated after this first reaping. All these changes had a particular meaning, and Isis changed her garments just as the earth changes its appearance.

If, beside an Isis carrying a crescent on her head and a sickle in her hand, the priests displayed to the assembled people an Osiris with his bushel <note>a container used for measuring grain, symbolizing abundance</note>, the poor could understand that there was a funeral sacrifice and an anniversary distribution at the new moon that must precede the harvest. A single example of this symbolic language suffices to make one understand how easily its meaning could be varied according to the situations and the attributes of the figures.

A philosopher, preoccupied with some physical system or sublime thoughts on the nature of spirits, will not fail, upon seeing the Egyptian <term>hieroglyphs: the "sacred carvings" or symbolic writing system of ancient Egypt</term>, to seek his favorite dogma there, and will believe he perceives it clearly. But let us have neither prejudices nor systems; they are nearly the same thing. When one knows the human heart, one easily guesses the meaning of a person’s actions by their needs; and it is by studying the needs of the Egyptian colony that one can reasonably interpret the lessons of Thoth <note>The Egyptian god of wisdom, writing, and the moon, often credited with inventing the arts and sciences</note>, and the meaning of the principal characters of the writing he devised for the service of the people.

Alongside public signs intended to communicate the annual cycle and the entire sequence of festivals, the people still needed others to be shown to them that could establish the order and timing of their various labors. This is what we shall call the **Rural Year**.

### OF THE HEAVENS.

->D ij<-

(The reader now understands this language;) after having represented the sun by the figure of a man or a governor, and the earth under the form of a woman or a fertile mother, the Egyptians designated labor by the figure of a child beloved by Osiris and Isis, a well-loved son whom they take pleasure in showering with gifts. Then, through the various forms they gave to this child—sometimes painting him as a grown man, or giving him the wings of certain winds, the horns of celestial animals, a club, or an arrow, and other such meaningful ornaments or instruments—they ingeniously expressed the conduct, the successive operations, the hardships, and the successes of <term>tillage: the preparation of land for growing crops</term>.

They gave this child the name of *Hores* or *Horos* (*a*), which apparently in Egyptian, as in Hebrew, Phoenician, and Arabic, equally signified the plowman and the craftsman, tillage and industry—in a word, labor. They often abbreviated his symbol to the simple painting of a human head, the seat <note>The text cuts off here, likely referring to the head as the seat of reason or direction.</note>—

Countless monuments of antiquity attest to the use of the portable chest, the winnowing fan, the child, and the serpent (a). To better explain how human industry had gradually repaired or softened the disorder caused by the flood <note>original: "le déluge"</note>, they added to these figures the wretched seeds upon which people had been forced to subsist in the beginning, and the signs of the hardships <note>original: "les marques des traverses"</note> that had to be overcome. The individuals who carried the chest containing all these memorials in the public ceremony also took on meaningful names and became part of the representation. They became actors <note>original: "actrices," though used here for the generic performers</note>, and everything, alongside the symbolic pieces, combined to reveal certain truths to the spectators.

The representative child was called simply "the Child," *the son* <note>original Latin: "liber"</note>, the well-beloved Son; sometimes "the Child, author of life or subsistence," *Father Liber* <note>original Latin: "liber Pater," an ancient Italian deity of growth and fertility</note>; sometimes "the Child of the representation," *the son of the image* <term>ben Séméléh: likely an etymological attempt to link the Greek "Semele" to the Hebrew "ben" (son) and "semel" (image or idol)</term>; sometimes Harpocrates, Bacchus, Apollo, or Icarus. **The Poetic Heaven.** Countless monuments from antiquity testify to the use of the portable casket, the winnowing basket <note>A "van" or winnowing basket was used in agriculture to separate grain from chaff; in ancient mysteries, it symbolized purification.</note>, the child, and the serpent $(a)$. The people who carried the casket containing all these memorials in public ceremonies also took on meaningful names and were part of the performance. They became actresses, and everything—combined with the symbolic objects—worked together to convey certain truths to the spectators.

### XIV.

->*Horus, or the symbols of the different labors of the year.*<-

These figures of Horus, in passing from the hands of one people into those of another, were undoubtedly diversified according to the whims of those who adopted these ceremonies, and gave rise to many fables. The truth of the interpretation we have just given to the figure of Horus can be justified by the detail of the various forms he was made to take, since they all tend to express some of the annual operations of husbandry, or the obstacles it must overcome, or the favors it experiences.

It is in this same spirit of agricultural utility that we must interpret the other variations of the figure. When he was shown with his feet tied, it was not to represent a captive or a crippled god, but to signify the period when the waters of the Nile became stagnant and "rested" upon the fields to deposit their fertile silt. 

### XV.

->*The transition from signs to gods.*<-

We see, therefore, how the most **thoughtful** arrangements of a wise and industrious people were gradually obscured. By losing the key to these symbols, the poets of later ages were forced to invent fables to explain the strange postures of these figures. What was once a calendar of labor became a genealogy of deities, and the respect once paid to a useful signal was transformed into the worship of an idol.

By its attributes, its gesture, and its name, this figure does not direct the minds of those present toward the idea of the sun, nor toward the respect required by sacrifice, nor toward the alleged secrecy of ancient mysteries; instead, it directs them toward the consideration of the abundance they enjoy during the winter, and toward the peaceful and moderate use of that abundance, which alone creates the happiness of society.

If this gesture of the finger placed upon the mouth of Harpocrates has deceived both the ancients and the moderns, it is because they judged the intent of this figure solely by its gesture; whereas they ought to have judged the meaning of the gesture by the attributes accompanying it, and by the functions expressed by its name. <gloss>(a)</gloss> Such were the cries: *io Bacché*, *hevoé Bacché*, *io triumphé*, *io pæan*. This word *io*, *jeov*, *jevoé*, *hevoé* is the name of God, and means *the author of life, the one who is* <note>The author is connecting these pagan cries to the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, YHWH.</note>. *Bacché* comes from <note>Hebrew: בכה (beche)</note> "weeping." *Triumphé* comes from <note>Hebrew: תרועה (teroweh)</note>, which Westerners pronounced as *triumphé*, there being no letter whose pronunciation was more difficult and varied than the <note>Hebrew letter ayin (ע)</note>. All these words, joined to the name of God, were short expressions by which the peoples exhorted one another to turn to God in their troubles, and to address their prayers and cries to Him. The whole was similar to those ways of speaking used by the Latins and the French: *Deo gratias* <note>Latin: "Thanks be to God"</note>, "God be thanked," or "adieu" <note>French: literally "to God," used as a parting blessing</note>.

It taught them to secure all kinds of healthy nourishment, to benefit from the labor of bees, to work the wool of sheep, and to make the most of all the productions of nature. The drum or the flute, which were inseparable from the celebration of these festivals, were symbols of the gratitude that brought men together on certain appointed days.

### *Living animals, having become symbolic.*

Now that we are acquainted with the preference of Eastern peoples, and especially the Egyptians, for symbolic figures, we are justified in believing that the singular practices observed among them were so many signs of certain truths—be they astronomical, moral, or otherwise. We no longer run a risk in stating that the ram honored in the Thebaid and in Libya, the bulls honored at Memphis and Heliopolis, the kids <note>young goats</note> honored at Mendes, the lion, the fish, and other animals honored in various regions, were in their origin very simple symbols. They were merely the ancient signs of the zodiac and the various markers of the sun’s positions. The new moon <term>neomenia: the religious celebration of the beginning of the lunar month</term> of one month or another was characterized by accompanying the figure of Isis—who announced this feast—with the sight of the celestial animal which the sun was then entering. Instead of a mere painting, the animal itself was made to appear in the festival—the living animal that corresponded to the sign. The dog being the symbol of the Dog Star <term>canicule: the star Sirius, whose rising heralded the hottest days of summer and the beginning of the Egyptian year</term> which formerly opened the year, they made a...

<header>OF THE HEAVENS.</header>

<margin>SYMBOLIC CEREMONIES.</margin>
...a living dog at the head of the entire ceremonial of the first new moon <term>neomenia: the religious celebration of the beginning of the lunar month</term>. It is Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> * who reports this to us as an eyewitness. People became accustomed to calling these new moons the feast of the ram, the feast <margin>* *Library, Book 1.* <note>original: "Biblioth. l. 1."</note></margin> of the bull, of the dog, or of the lion. The new moon of the ram quite naturally became the most solemn in those places where there was a great trade in sheep. The new moon of the bull was the most pleasant of all in the rich pastures of Memphis and Lower Egypt. The festival of the sun’s entry into the kids <note>young goats; referring to the sun's position in the zodiac</note> was magnificent at Mendes, where more goats were raised than elsewhere. Each city thus grew fond of the new moon of one sign or another, according to the interest or the preference they might find there. In the custom of decorating the ceremonial with singular figures, the people would crown with flowers and lead in procession the symbolic animal whose name the festival bore. Could they fail to look upon the very object that constituted their special wealth with a particular fondness? It is true that after the introduction of idolatry, they refrained from killing the animal they had seen appear so honorably in their ceremonies. But they nevertheless always continued to trade in them.

The people of Mendes honored goats and ate sheep. Those of Thebes honored sheep and ate goats. One can therefore suspect, as most scholars do, that utility and commercial interest were the motives that led the Egyptians to cherish these animals, and why seeing them was so gratifying during their festivals. But however plausible this conjecture about the origin of revered animals in Egypt may be, here is something more certain regarding this bizarre custom, about which so much has been written without ever identifying its true origin. M. de Maillet <note>Benoît de Maillet (1656–1738) was a French diplomat whose posthumous "Description de l'Égypte" provided Europe with detailed accounts of Egyptian life and geography.</note> in his *Description of Egypt*, which he knew intimately after a stay of more than sixteen years, informs us that the harvest takes place in May in Lower Egypt; in April above Cairo; and in March, or even earlier, in Upper Egypt. As the harvest is the event that most powerfully moves the spirit of a people, the new moon festival <term>neomenia: a religious celebration marking the beginning of the lunar month</term> that concluded the wheat harvest could not fail to be one of the most joyful of all their celebrations. From this comes the great solemnity of the sun's entry into the Ram <note>the zodiac sign of Aries; original: "bélier"</note> in the vicinity of Thebes. The granary was full: that says everything. The transport boat was named *tranquility* (b), because it only transported the righteous; and on the contrary, the boatman who refused without quarter those whom the judges had not acquitted, was named *wrath* (c), or vengeance.

As for the earth thrown on the body and the tender farewells of the relatives, it was a natural duty and the simple expression of their regrets. But they were not content with rendering this honor in passing over the grave: they placed at the entrance of the cemetery and above the door of the deceased the symbol of the esteem and tender affection they bore for their dead relative. The dog, being the animal most attached to man, is the natural symbol of friendship.

# HISTORY

<margin>THE POETIC SKY.</margin>
The advantage derived from writing and symbolic ceremonies made their use more frequent and widespread day by day: but people soon found themselves stopped by an inconvenience that was inseparable from them. Regardless of the care taken to limit the number of symbols, and to skillfully make the same character or the same <term>key<note>In early studies of linguistics, "keys" (clés) referred to what we now call radicals in Chinese characters—the component parts used to categorize and organize written signs.</note></term> serve a multitude of things that shared some relationship; by adding, removing, or merely varying an attribute or a piece of the symbolic figure (as is still practiced in Chinese writing); it was realized that this writing would eventually become almost impracticable due to the sheer quantity of figures. These had to be multiplied or varied just as objects are, and even as the judgments the mind makes about these objects. This is still today the great inconvenience of Chinese writing, which depicts not the sounds of the voice, but the objects of thought, through a multitude of different characters or keys, and by the innumerable variations with which each key is burdened.

<margin>THE BIRTH OF THE GODS.</margin> [The inventor] lived before the age of Job and Moses; an attentive spirit, a fortunate genius whose name history has not preserved for us, who, having noticed that the sounds of the voice with which we can signify everything we please are quite few in number, took it upon himself to represent this small number of sounds by an equal number of characters. From this, it followed that by representing with twenty or twenty-four letters the twenty or twenty-four primary sounds and articulations—which are sufficient through their mixing to form words, or the signs of objects—one could, with very few characters, give rise to the thought of all the things we distinguish by the diversity of these sounds.

This invention, so simple and so fertile, met with rapid success. It passed to the Arabs, was communicated to the Hebrews, then to the Phoenicians, and by the latter to the Greeks, and from there to the inhabitants of the Isles: it even penetrated as far as the peoples of the North. The new writing, formed from a very small number of characters representative of sounds, suddenly awakened the thought of the object—or the judgment attached to that sound—alongside the idea of the sound itself.

This [phonetic script] became, in Egypt and everywhere else, the current and popular writing. No other was used in the affairs of society, because it was easy to learn and, furthermore, provided a very efficient service.

Symbolic writing <note>The author refers here to the earliest form of Egyptian writing, which used pictures to represent ideas or sounds.</note>, which from its very beginning was tied to religion, astronomy, and the ordinances that regulated society, found itself consecrated by the honorable use that had been made of it initially. This was true both in the places and instruments destined for religious worship, and in the lessons given by masters to their disciples. It continued to be employed in festivals, on tombs, and on public monuments. It became the writing of the learned and the priests. It was preserved in certain schools, and even more so in the outward practice of religion, whose ceremonial—once established—is perpetuated without it being easy to change or modify. To promote the value of the new writing, it was not felt necessary to erase the figures of the old that were found on the sacred tablets, on the large vessels used for making offerings, on obelisks, on tombs, and generally on everything relating to piety and instruction.

->I.<-

### *God, the sun, and Osiris conflated.*

<margin>
How the ideas of God and the sun became conflated.

Since the sun served as the physical "body" of this symbol, they called it the sun; however, as the All-Powerful Being was the "soul" or the underlying meaning of the literal symbol, they also called this figure *the Being*, *the Eternal*, *the Father of Life*, *the Strong*, and *the Most High* (a), rather than simply naming it the sun. It was primarily before this figure that they prostrated themselves during their sacrifices. They addressed their thanks and their prayers to the Most High, whom this script was intended to keep present in their minds. But because the eye, the ear, and the mind were constantly occupied with the image of the sun during public religious acts, the common people eventually transferred all these exalted titles, their gratitude, and their adoration to the sun itself. As soon as God was confused with His own handiwork, this initial illusion opened the door to a thousand other extravagances.

What most seduced the Egyptians—who were struck by the singular attire of this woman <note>Referring to the figure of Isis, who originated as a symbolic harvest sign or "public notice" before being worshipped as a goddess.</note> always present in their assemblies—was the frequent union of a crescent or a full moon with her headdresses. They took this as an opportunity to proclaim that the wife of Osiris, the common mother of the Egyptians, had the moon for her dwelling. The festivals of the Most High <note>The author suggests that religious feasts were originally intended for the one supreme God before they were diverted to celestial bodies.</note> had been fixed to the new moon <term>neomenia: the beginning of the lunar month</term>, or the full moon, or a specific part of the waning phase, only because these phases were a natural indication and an easy way to gather the people on an agreed-upon and announced day. They lost sight of the Adorable Being, the sole object of these festivals; they believed them to be consecrated to the moon itself, and to that imaginary woman whom they believed resided there, being very attentive to their needs. Even the spots on the moon, which by a false appearance of a human face, served to strengthen their illusion.

Seeking, therefore, to understand their Horus from a historical perspective, the connection this symbol had with the regulations of farming and the calendar led them to take him for Menes, the founder of all public order. In the belief that this meaningful figure was not only a real person, but indeed one of their ancestors—deified and dwelling in heaven—and that he was the son of Ham, their legislator Menes, they named him sometimes Chemmis \*, sometimes Osiris the younger, or simply Osiris; and by combining the names of the father and the son into one, they called him Maneros and Menosiris \*, or, in allusion to the Nile, Mnevis and Menophis †. ### V.

->*The propagation of Egyptian gods. The progress of idolatry.*<-

Having found, in the misuse of symbolic figures taken for real objects, the origin of the inhabitants whom Egypt imagined and placed in the heavens, if it also turns out that the gods of other nations, and the other superstitions we have not yet discussed, are a clear propagation of Egyptian ideas and practices; then the ease of tracing so many errors back to one very simple principle will again demonstrate the accuracy of that principle, even though it already seems sufficiently proven.

But is it so easy to prove that the Phoenicians, the Syrians, the Greeks, and all the Westerners were the copyists of the Egyptians? The latter traveled little. Usually content with the abundance they enjoyed at home, they could do without foreigners *(a)*, and did not go searching elsewhere for what they gathered without effort in their own country. For this reason, they might seem poorly suited to serve as models for other peoples, or to communicate their opinions to them. It is nevertheless Egypt that spread idolatry and superstitions everywhere. <header>HISTORY IX. THE POETIC HEAVEN.</header>

### The chariot of the sun, the equipages of the gods.

The whip that was placed in the hand of Osiris, in the right hand of the Jupiter of Heliopolis (who is the same deity), and in the right hand of the Jupiter of Syria *(a)*, who is no different, clearly made this god the charioteer <term>cocher: while today this suggests a simple driver, in antiquity it referred to the noble art of the charioteer</term> or the guide of the year, the stars, and all of nature. The idea of a charioteer had nothing base about it then; on the contrary, governing a chariot was a very honorable function in antiquity. It was the cherished exercise of kings and the greatest <margin>* See Homer’s *Iliad*.</margin> warriors *. The Greeks, more imaginative than other peoples, when adopting the figure of the sun, were not satisfied with simply putting a whip in his hand; rather, to the whip—which was quite sufficient to signify the guidance of the year in the ancient writing <note>The author likely refers to hieroglyphic or symbolic communication</note>—they added a chariot, horses <margin>* See Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book 2.</margin> full of fire, and a complete equipage *. They depicted their sun-god with a

---

> *(a) Right hand raised with a whip in the manner of a charioteer.* <note>original Latin: "Dextra elevata cum flagro in aurigæ modum."</note> Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter 23. The author calls this Jupiter "Assyrian." But "Assyrian" in this passage stands for "Syrian," as can be judged by his name *Adad*, which was the name for God in Syria, and was part of the names of the kings of that country, such as *Benadad* <note>Ben-Hadad</note>. The same mistake is found in Virgil and Horace.

### THEOGONY.

It was anciently a universal custom to perform sacrifices and public prayers on high places, and especially in large woods, to shield the people from the heat of the sun. When the symbol of Isis—which indicated the festivals and whose figures formed one of the most beautiful parts of the ceremonial—became the object of worship itself, she came to be regarded as the dispenser of the goods of the earth, the marks of which she always carried. ### XI.

->*Deio, Dione, Diana, Hecate, Artemisia.*<-

It has always been true, in every land, that the common people love ambiguities and puns. If the changing of a figure's appearance often turned a single varied symbol into several different gods, the mere diversity of names—or even a simple difference in pronunciation—often produced a similar multiplicity. **Isis**, when taken for the queen of heaven or for the moon, was named *Echet*, *Hecate*, or *Achate*, meaning *the unique* or *the excellent* (*a*). Among certain peoples of Syria, the same symbol, through a slight inflection of the name, was called *Achot* (*b*), meaning *the sister*. To take it rightly, the moon was only placed in the sky to be consulted by men regarding what they must do; since the Creator gave it different phases only to be, in the heavens, the public measure of time and the sensible <note>In the 18th-century sense: "perceptible to the senses" or "evident."</note> rule for all labors. ### XII.

#### *Cybele.*

The Isis we have just seen is a maiden of severe virtue, whose virginity is beyond all suspicion. Let us pass into Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>: there, according to the tastes of the people, this same Isis takes on a completely different character. She is honored there as the common mother of all the gods. She is carried in triumph through the cities as the model of an admirable fertility; and the people congratulate her for having all the gods of the first rank as her children, and for being able to embrace a hundred grandsons (*a*).

The towers with which she is crowned allow us to recognize her as an Egyptian Isis—the ancient symbol of the gratitude that people must show during festivals to the one who provides them with the means to feed, clothe, and house themselves. The drums or flutes that accompany Cybele were the characteristic markers of a festival: and since the principal festival or assembly that concerned all the different peoples (who were distinct from the Egyptians) was the one held in summer to mark the beginning of the harvest, it was designated

Ever since greed, sanctioned by custom, had converted the most disordered pleasures into so many acts of devotion, the temples and groves of the goddess of generation were filled with young women who resided there. <margin>THE THEOGONY.</margin> others are the most jealous? One undoubtedly finds nothing but contradictions and difficulties when attempting to assign to each their rightful department and prevent quarrels. But our explanation, which traces them all back to Isis <note>the Egyptian mother goddess, whom the author sees as the "original" version of all these female deities</note>, easily reconciles these disputes. Juno, Venus, and Diana thus have the same pretensions; and their jurisdictional conflicts here attest to the unity of their origin. All are derived from the symbol of the festivals where God was praised for the effects of His fecundity.

But why was the Isis of Sais armed? Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> can help us find the answer. He adds that it was solely from the class of laborers that all the soldiers were drawn. The inhabitants of Sais, who were all from the class of laborers and solely occupied with the cultivation of the olive tree—and among the most distinguished for the number of good soldiers they provided—preferred to honor the armed Isis, or the goddess as she was anciently dressed to announce the recruitment or the march of troops.

A new proof that this so-called warrior was only a public notice <note>The author argues that ancient gods were originally symbolic signs (affiches) used to announce agricultural events.</note> is that the inhabitants of Sais usually joined to the breastplate or the shield of their Isis another attribute, which was also merely the announcement or the advertisement of their great festival—the particular festival of their district. This solemnity, where the inhabitants of Sais praised God for providing them with abundance through the fruit of the olive tree, was celebrated in the evening, at the full moon, after the pressing of the olives. They marked the beginning of the night and the nocturnal sacrifice with an owl, which is accustomed to leaving its nest at that time. They expressed the circumstance of the full moon by placing a full moon upon the head or the breast of Isis. To make it understood that the intention of the sacrifice was to praise God for having given them their sustenance through the excellent oil they gathered, they surrounded this face, or this moon, with several serpents, common symbols of life; and there was so little mystery in this that, to better understand the whole thing, they gave this announcement the name of *Medusa*, which meant quite simply the *pressing of the olives* (a).

But how did a figure intended to signify such simple things become transformed into a monster capable of freezing with terror those who looked upon it? The Greek sculptors understood nothing of the meaning of the serpents surrounding Medusa, which were actually symbols for the announcement *of the pressing*. They did not believe they should give graceful features to a head that bore such a hairstyle. This ugliness of the features, combined with the appearance of the serpents, gave free rein to the poets' imaginations. It was said of the pressing process that it turned fruit into stone. ### XVI.

->*Minos.*<-

Let us move from the mainland to one of the most beautiful islands in the Mediterranean, and one of the first encountered upon leaving Egypt—I mean the island of Crete. The practice has been perpetuated from age to age. The early Christians, so careful to avoid all superstition, would assemble every year to pray and to celebrate the Holy Sacrifice <note>The Eucharist or Mass</note> upon the tombs of the Martyrs. Ever since Egypt became obsessed with the ridiculous idea that the statues of Osiris, Isis, and Horus—which served to regulate society through their respective meanings—were monuments to their founders; that Osiris had lived in Egypt and had been buried there; they fabricated stories consistent with this belief. One easily sees how they were of a nature to appear as so many monuments of past events when taken literally, and that they have no more historical reality in Egypt than they do elsewhere. This point of criticism, shedding new light on all that has preceded it, is worth clarifying further and strengthening with other circumstances that finally demonstrate its certainty.

It is because the Cretans derived their origins and religious customs from Egypt that they initially possessed a labyrinth—or a palace—divided into as many chambers as there were months in the year. In these rooms, significant figures <note>symbolic statues or icons representing astronomical or seasonal changes</note> relating to each month were placed to teach the young priests being raised there about the order of the heavens and Egyptian governance <term>police: refers here to the civil regulations and organized administration of society</term>. ### XVII.

->*Dionysius, Bacchus.*<-

In the era when people expressed themselves through symbols, and varied their elements to make themselves understood—far from intending to hide any mystery—the figure of Horus <note>In this context, the author uses Horus as a primary symbolic figure representing the sun or seasonal cycles.</note> changed names and attributes according to the specific needs of the situation in which it was used. The first use made of it in certain festivals was *the representation of the past*. The second was for instruction and *the regulations suitable for the people*.

---

(*a*) One may also observe here that the Cretan Minos is not a man who actually existed, since his colleagues Rhadamanthus and Aeacus are merely two words that signified things entirely different from men, though their original meanings were no longer known. Since the name Menes or Minos had been commonly used to signify a funeral assembly; when speaking of the judgment which in Crete, as in Egypt, was required to precede burial, it was called the *judgment of death*, the *judgment of sorrow*, or the *judgment of those who sleep*, or the *judgment of the long sleep*. Now, all of this was expressed by the three words *Minos*, *Aeacus*, and *Rhadamanthus*. Minos and the *manes* <note>The *manes* refers to the ancestral spirits of the dead in Roman religion; the author links this to the concept of a "funeral assembly."</note> were understood in the same sense to mean the funeral assembly, or death. **עקה** <note>Hebrew: *aaca*</note> *aaca* signifies the most bitter sorrow; **רדמימ** <note>Hebrew: *redamim*</note> *redamim* signifies those who sleep deeply; and **רדמת** <note>Hebrew: *redamet*</note> *redamet* signifies the great sleep.

The title among them all that was most used in Italy was Bacchoth. The delicate ears of the Greeks, who were enemies of harsh sounds, adapted better to the name Dionysus. These various titles—and the list of them was long—gave rise to just as many stories. Thus, they gave this god the name Dionysus because he was the son of Jov or Jupiter, and because he had been born at Nysa, a city in Arabia. He was the son of Cush, and consequently a descendant of Ham, the father of the latter. He came from Khuzestan <note>A province in southwestern Iran; the author notes the linguistic connection between "Cush" and "Khuzestan."</note>, a province beyond the Persian Gulf which, as one can see, still preserves the name of Nimrod's father. This provided the occasion to conflate Nimrod with Bacchus, and to attribute to Bacchus a great hunt and famous victories beyond the Tigris, stretching as far as the Indies. The resemblance between Bacchus and Nimrod is based on the fact that the festivals bearing the name of Bacchus are representations of ancient hunts, and that Nimrod had been a mighty hunter who often led the youth in pursuit of dangerous wild animals, delivering the country by renewing these hunts every three years. The description that Holy Scripture <note>Referring to the Book of Genesis in the Bible.</note> gives us of Nimrod supports this connection. It says he was called pre-eminently: *the mighty hunter before the Lord*, or the hunter whose undertakings God blessed. I do not know on what basis the scholars' outcry against <note>The text cuts off here; the author is likely beginning a defense of Nimrod against theologians who traditionally viewed him as a tyrant or rebel against God.</note>

Time and experience taught men to spin sheep's wool and goat hair, providing themselves with softer clothing that was easier to wash.

When the arts were invented and perfected through new trials, the memory of the coarseness of the earliest ages—and the comparison of the hardships mankind first endured with the conveniences and inventions of later times—made the rural festivals, or the *festivals representing the ancient state*, more spirited than all others.

One of the most essential elements of this festival was, therefore, to appear covered in the skins of goats, deer, tigers, or other animals, whether domestic or wild. They would smear their faces with blood to carry the marks of the danger they had faced and the victory they had achieved.

Instead of blood, they often had recourse to a light coating of wine lees <note>The sediment or dregs found at the bottom of a wine cask.</note>, or to mulberry juice, which, when spread across a face, was slightly less disgusting to the actor than animal blood would have been, yet served to decorate just as well.

2°. After the representation of the ancient state of the human race—the meaning of which was entirely perverted by the transformation of these symbolic figures into so many gods—the festivals of Horus, or of <term>tilling the soil</term> <note>The original French *labourage* refers specifically to plowing and the systematic cultivation of the earth.</note>, still contained the various lessons or regulations for the annual labors, the beginnings and duration of which were important for the people to know. This is what was announced to them in this festival and in others through the various garments or attributes given to Horus. Every wind, every operation, every precaution born of experience had its own mark and its own sign. We shall not repeat what we have said about them; but what is necessary to remark here is that the <term>Menes</term> <note>A name likely referring to the legendary first Pharaoh, interpreted here by the author as a symbol for social order and law.</note>, or the symbol of the regulations of society, became the teacher of the human race, the <term>lawgiver Bacchus</term> (*a*).

It is, finally, the symbol of <term>tilling the soil</term> <note>The French *labourage* implies the entire system of agricultural labor that anchors a civilization.</note>, and not any man who had ever lived, who gave lessons to all families; and by placing a fingertip to his lips, delivered the most salutary of all sermons to whoever would listen. ### XX.

#### *Hercules.*

When predatory animals became too numerous, or when there was some savage beast or a notorious thief disturbing the region, then they would summon not an entire army, nor a new levy of recruits, but only those most experienced in the trade of war—those who had acquired the most distinguished ranks, or *perhaps volunteers*, those who presented themselves without compulsion for the expedition. I judge the intention of this symbol by the name that was given to it. We know <note>The OCR "fait" is likely "sait" (knows).</note> from the reports of Herodotus, Diodorus, Plutarch, and many other ancients, that study was the primary duty of the priests of Egypt, who led very secluded lives. They applied themselves to understanding the order of the stars, the course of the celestial bodies and of the year, the movements of the air, and the return of certain winds, the flooding of the Nile, the tides of the Arabian Gulf <note>A historical name for the Red Sea.</note>, the layout of continents, islands, countries, and distant seas, the succession of festivals, the specific cycle of the moon, eclipses, the appearance of planets and stars, geometry, and especially land surveying: in short, they engaged in a diligent and arduous study of the earth, the sea, the heavens, and all of nature. This is apparently what was meant by the Horus surnamed Atlas. Let us judge this by the name, the figure, and the transformations to which his name and image have given rise.

<margin>The Garden of the Hesperides.</margin>
Among the other fables that Phoenician <note>An ancient seafaring civilization from the Levant, famous for their trade and navigation across the Mediterranean.</note> travelers had plenty of leisure to imagine during their journeys, or to recount upon their return, the two most beautiful, without doubt, are those of the Garden of the Hesperides and that of Atlas being relieved by Hercules of the burden of the celestial globe. What might be the origin of the first? Three nymphs placed around a tree that produces golden apples, and mistresses in control of this marvelous fruit; a dragon that watches to prevent any other from using or accessing it; a wild goat grazing at the foot of the tree; or finally, instead of the goat, a horn of plenty placed either at the foot of the tree or in the hand of one of the three nymphs: such is the representation of the Garden of the Hesperides.

This seemingly fabulous depiction is but the ancient symbol of the riches of Tarshish <note>A biblical and historical region, often associated with Tartessos in southern Spain, renowned for its mineral wealth.</note>. The three nymphs appear to be the three *Isises* <note>The author refers to "Isis" here as symbolic public markers or personified months rather than just the Egyptian goddess.</note>, or the announcements of three months during which it was favorable to set sail for trade in Hesperia <note>The "Western Land," a term used by the ancients to refer to Italy or the Iberian Peninsula.</note> or of

### XXIII.

->*Eros, Love, and Hymen.*<-

No one is unaware that it was a universal custom in antiquity to go, on the wedding day, to meet the groom and the bride with lamps and torches. The friends of the groom carried a torch made of resinous wood; the young women who were friends of the bride carried a lamp. There is no one who has not read and admired the delightful description that the Gospel <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 25.</note> gives of the procession of the latter, and it is unnecessary to cite anything further. Everyone awaited the moment when the groom would be ready to go and fetch the bride from her parents' house, and to bring her to his own with all the men and women who were to accompany her and be admitted into the banquet hall. As soon as he appeared, the two choirs of young people...

This young man bore the name of Hymenaeus, which means *here is the festival (a), here is the groom who comes*.

This may seem at first to be mere conjecture. However, let us observe that the custom of making joyful or mournful announcements through various decorations on doorways has been passed down to us from the most remote antiquity. The niches intended to hold certain symbols or the markers of a festival—whether at the corners of crossroads or above the doors of private homes—have been put to another use among us, yet they can still be found. The markers of the labor of each season, joined with the nuptial torch, came to be seen as the monuments of his victories. He had disarmed all the gods, and their attributes in his hands became the subject of the poets' playfulness, and then of the profound reflections of the philosophers, who were a thousand times more ridiculous on this subject than the poets.

Since the introduction of idolatry, the Egyptians—who hated the sea—did not honor Neptune: but they preserved his name, which signifies *the arrival of the fleet*, and gave it to the extremities of Egypt, or to the seashore. It is Plutarch <note>A famous Greek historian and essayist (c. 46 – 119 AD).</note> who reports this to us. Proteus going to the borders of Egypt, and toward Pharos, to count the sea-steeds and provide them with everything, can be nothing other than the sale of Egyptian commodities that was carried out at Pharos upon the arrival of the Phoenician barks. The name of Proteus confirms it. It signifies nothing other than *the abundance of fruits, or the productions of the earth* (a).

Four neglected quarter-days made one full day at the end of four years; and by neglecting to <term>intercalate</term> <note>To insert an extra day into a calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year, much like our modern leap year.</note> a day after those four years—or to count 366 days instead of 365—their civil year began one day too early. By moving backward, it drifted by the value of an entire day from the calculation of the natural year. It drifted by two days after eight years, and by three after twelve years. Thus, the opening of the sacred year traveled successively through every day of the calendar over a duration of 365 times four years, which makes 1,460 years <note>This period is known to historians as the Sothic Cycle.</note>. In the catalogs of the ancient kings of Egypt drawn from **Manetho**, **Eratosthenes**, and **Syncellus** <note>These were influential ancient chroniclers and historians whose works are primary sources for Egyptian dynastic history.</note>, and carefully collected in Marsham's rule of times <note>Sir John Marsham was a 17th-century English writer known for his work on Egyptian chronology, *Canon Chronicus*.</note>, one finds the invention of writing attributed equally to **Thoth** and to Aesculapius. Marsham is annoyed by this and corrects these misunderstandings as best he can, persuaded as he is that Thoth and Aesculapius are two very different kings. But should one seriously treat a history where it is evident that two men—one reigning at **Thebes**, the other at **Memphis**—are made out of two names that both signify the dog star, and which were never given to any man who actually lived?

> (*a*) The proof of this custom is found frequently in Holy Scripture. When the prophetess Deborah, in her song <note>Referencing the Song of Deborah in Judges 5.</note>, congratulates the captains or the leaders of the half-tribe of Manasseh who lived beyond the Jordan for coming to the aid of the people of God against the enemy; she represents them to us as having their staff of command in hand. When the Tribes murmured at seeing the priesthood remain in the family of Aaron, the leaders of the tribes were ordered to bring their sceptre to the tabernacle. That of Levi, which was carried by Aaron, was found to have blossomed the next day, and Scripture notes that the other leaders each took back their own sceptre, or their staff of command. This distinction was so specifically assigned to the leader of each great family that in Oriental languages <note>The author refers to Hebrew and related Semitic languages.</note>, a tribe has no other name than that of the **sceptre** <note>original: "shebet" (שֵׁבֶט), which means both "staff/sceptre" and "tribe."</note> to which it is subordinate. Thus, the twelve sceptres of Jacob signify the twelve tribes of the Israelites; and to say the tribe of Levi, or the tribe of Judah, one could not say it otherwise than the sceptre of Levi, the staff of Judah. The ceremonies of each season, and the particular festivals that preceded or followed each harvest, had specific names to distinguish them. However, the general name of *manes*—meaning standards or images—remained attached to the funeral assemblies, which occurred frequently. Thus, the names of *manes*, images, likenesses, and the dead became conflated. Mercury, who performed the *opening and closing* of the manes <margin>(a)</margin>, became in this way the conductor of the dead. He led the souls with his wand held high. Whether king or shepherd, one had to follow the troop: he opened the somber abode for them, closed it without mercy, and turned the key without allowing anyone to leave <margin>(b)</margin>. This is also what the Phoenicians and the Arcadians meant when they called him the Cyllenian <margin>(c)</margin>. This word signified the closure, or the one who ends the year and who forever finishes the duration of life.

# HISTORY
<page-num>272</page-num>

<margin>THE POETIC HEAVENS.</margin>
By the history of Daedalus, and by that of our two Icaruses <note>The author distinguishes between Icarus the son of Daedalus and Icarius of Attica, the legendary bringer of wine.</note>, it is easy to judge how much mythology is a suspect foundation, and what mistakes one can make by seeking historical facts within it, since the people themselves are as unreal as their adventures.

<unclear>O</unclear>thers <note>Original Latin: *utres plenos in plaustrum impossuisse: hac re etiam Booten appellatum...*</note> say that he placed full skins of wine upon a wagon, and for this reason he was even called Boötes <note>From the Greek for "ox-driver" or "wagoner," identifying him with the constellation near the Great Bear.</note>. While traveling through the borders of Attica to show this gift to the shepherds, some among them, filled with greed and lulled into a deep sleep by this new kind of drink, were overcome. As some fell one way and others another, tossing their limbs about as if half-dead and speaking unbecomingly, the rest of them, believing that poison had been given to the shepherds by Icarius, threw him into a well.... But Erigone, the daughter of Icarius, moved by longing for her parent when she saw he did not return, tried to find him. Icarius's dog, whose name was Maera, returned to Erigone howling.... the timid girl could not help but suspect her father had been killed, having been absent for so many days and months.... as soon as the daughter saw the body, having lost all hope and overwhelmed by loneliness and poverty.... she ended her life by hanging. After she died, the dog gave up its spirit over its master.... Jupiter, pitying their misfortune, transformed their bodies into stars. Thus, many have called Icarius "Boötes" and Erigone "the Virgin" <note>The constellation Virgo.</note>. The dog, by its own name and appearance, they called the "Canicula" <note>The "Little Dog" or Sirius.</note>. 

Hyginus <note>Gaius Julius Hyginus, a Roman mythographer and librarian under Emperor Augustus.</note> then relates the misfortunes that befell the Athenians in punishment for the murder of Icarius, and the establishment of expiatory sacrifices, where they represented the sad accident and the poverty of Erigone as she went from place to place with the dog Maera searching for her father. He adds: *Furthermore, the rising of the Dog Star used to deprive their lands and fields of fruit due to the heat.... their king Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene.... asked his parent by what means he might free the city from this calamity. The God commanded him to appease the death of Icarius with many sacrifices and to ask Jove that, during the time the Dog Star rose, he might grant forty days of wind to moderate the heat of the star. Aristaeus fulfilled this command and obtained from Jove that the Etesian winds should blow.* One finds the same tale in the *Dionysiaca* of Nonnus <note>A massive Greek epic poem by Nonnus of Panopolis (5th century AD) detailing the life of Dionysus.</note>.

Yet one finds it somewhat difficult to accept the idea that Daedalus is nothing more than an Egyptian emblem <note>The author refers to the theory that many Greek myths were originally Egyptian symbols for agriculture or the stars.</note> converted, like so many others, into a character of extraordinary events. Through the fables and the wondrous tales for which the Phoenicians and Greeks were so eager, do we not find historical reality? All the ancients agree that Daedalus was an industrious architect. He is credited with the honor of inventing the <term>compass</term> <note>a tool for drawing circles and measuring distances</note> and the <term>square</term> <note>a tool used to create perfect right angles in building</note>. It is added that it is to him that we owe the art of statuary, and the nature of the progress this fine art began to make under his influence is even characterized by details that make the account extremely credible. *Until Daedalus*, as reported by Diodorus Siculus *(a)*, *statues had their eyes closed and their hands fixed to their sides. But Daedalus taught how to give them open eyes, to keep the legs separated, and to detach the hands from the body. This is what made him admired.*

---

*(a)* The craftsmen before him fashioned statues with their eyes closed <note>original Greek/Latin: *nictitantes* (blinking or closing the eyes)</note>, and with hands hanging down and stuck to their sides. But he (Daedalus) was the first to give them sight <note>original Latin: *oculis statuas instruens* (furnishing statues with eyes)</note> and to make the legs stepping forward, and furthermore, by making the hands extended, he was rightly admired among men. *Diodorus Siculus, Library, Book 4.*

The cessation of rustic labors could not be better represented than by a swaddled Horus, deprived of the use of his feet by the flood; he employed his arms only to display the measurement of the water, an instrument for gauging the wind, another for taking angles, and a horn to announce the general <term>surveying</term> <note>Original: "arpentage." These grand ideas may have come with time. But we are concerned here with the first practical use of the hook.

But after the flight of *Daedalus* <note>The author uses "Daedalus" as a symbolic name for a technical or astronomical marker used to signal that the waters were deep enough for irrigation</note>, that is to say, after Anubis—by the breath of the Etesian winds <note>The Etesian winds are strong, periodic Mediterranean winds that blow from the north, helping to push the Nile's waters inland</note> continuing for many days—had procured *a suitable depth of water*, the statues of Isis and Horus were presented in a more liberated form. The laborer recovered his eyes, his feet, and his arms. Here, then, is the origin of our admirable <term>statuary</term> <note>The art of making statues; the author argues that the development of movable limbs in sculpture began with these seasonal Egyptian signals</note>. It is true that later on, the Egyptians, no longer understanding the meaning of these symbols—which the ancient ritual caused to reappear during their festivals—sought great mysteries within them, and particularly multiplied those swaddled figures which had a more singular appearance than the others, such that they are found everywhere (*a*). But one sees by their very multitude that they belong to later times, and they do not justify in the least the reality of the story of Daedalus. As for the ideas that the Egyptians attached to these swaddling cloths, we concern ourselves little with them.

<margin>THE THEOGONY.</margin> These are all follies that related to the imaginary histories of their gods, or to allegories that were equally imaginary and just as recent.

One would rightly complain of my silence if I neglected to respond to the objection drawn from the famous statue of Memnon <note>The Colossi of Memnon are two massive stone statues of Pharaoh Amenhotep III; in antiquity, the northern statue was famous for producing a "singing" sound at dawn</note> or Menophis, which, according to the account of Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), a Greek sophist who wrote about the life of Apollonius of Tyana, including descriptions of the Memnon statue</note>, had its feet joined together in a block, and which spoke or resonated at sunrise. Who does not see that this is a statue of Horus taken historically for Menes or Menof <note>The author equates the god Horus with Menes, traditionally considered the first human King of Egypt and its primary legislator</note>, the legislator of Egypt? If it was said that this figure had such a great sympathy with the sun, it is because, in effect, Horus was intended for nothing else than to warn the laborers of what they had to do each day of the year. He had nothing to say to them for the night. His lessons were only to regulate what had to be done according to the season at each sunrise. From this, people took the opportunity to say, at first jokingly and later quite seriously, that it was a speaking statue, and that its voice could be heard at the rising of the sun.

Thus, one often finds in the writings of ancient authors that the Cabiri <note>A group of enigmatic deities honored in mystery cults across the ancient Greek world</note> were identified as Jupiter, Ceres, and Bacchus, or the younger Dionysus.

Often they add a fourth, whom they name sometimes Mercury, sometimes Cadmillus—or Casmillus and Camillus—which among the Etruscans <note>The civilization in central Italy that preceded the Romans</note> and in Latium <note>The region surrounding Rome</note> signified a minister or a messenger. That is to say, we find here once again the four principal keys of the ancient Egyptian writing <note>The author refers to the symbolic images or hieroglyphs used to signal seasonal events</note>, changed, because of their human form, into as many *tutelary and powerful* gods.

An Egyptian or Phoenician colony, which utilized all these symbolic figures in the ceremonies of its religion, transported them into Phocis <note>A region in central Greece.</note> in the vicinity of Mount Parnassus and Delphi. In that new land, they no longer carried any meaning; they had no relation to anything suited to the country—that much is true. To everything that has just been said, one may add the fable of the dispute between Athena <note>original: "Pallas-Athéné."</note> and Neptune <note>The Roman name for the sea god Poseidon.</note> to determine which of the two would offer a more beautiful gift to the new city, and thereby deserve to give it their name. It signified either the two means the Athenians had for their subsistence—namely, agriculture and navigation—or the preference they ought to give to agriculture over navigation. Two or three examples of this kind can sufficiently clarify all those ancient figures that Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century CE Greek traveler whose "Description of Greece" serves as a primary source for ancient landmarks.</note> details for us in his description of Greece, along with the fables that resulted from them.

### XXIX.

->*The Furies, the Fates, and the Harpies.*<-

The distribution we have just seen of the twelve Isises <note>The author uses "Isis" as a generic term for the female figures or statues used in the Egyptian calendar system.</note> into three Graces—or three idle nymphs who are led by Mercury <note>The author likely refers to the "Anubis" or "Hermes" figure as a signal for the Nile's rising.</note>—and nine other active nymphs who are led by Horus, is confirmed by another distribution which, as different as it may seem, has a precise correspondence with the previous one. This is the division into three Graces, three Furies, three Fates, and three Harpies. This second dozen of such strange figures is once again nothing more than the sequence of the Egyptian months, characterized according to the seasons.

The Graces <note>original: "Charites"</note> are, as we have just seen, the Isises or the markers of the months of July, August, and September.

The Furies, or the Eumenides <note>A Greek name for the Furies meaning "the kindly ones," used as a euphemism to avoid their wrath.</note>, with their heads surrounded by serpents and torches in their fists, seemed suited in Greece only for tormenting the wicked in Tartarus <note>In Greek mythology, the deepest part of the underworld where the wicked are punished.</note>. This is the role that the poets assign to them, unless they make them emerge to inspire some evil deed or to drive nations to madness.

All of these fables are based upon their physical appearance:

### XXX.

->*Bellerophon, Perseus, Andromeda.*<-

I do not doubt that my reader may be a little surprised to find the Harpies changed into insects, to see the Furies become the announcements of wine-pressing, and to encounter the symbol of navigation upon the rocks of Parnassus <note>A mountain in Greece sacred to Dionysus and the Muses. The author argues that symbols like Pegasus, often associated with this site, were originally maritime or agricultural signs.</note>: but the singularity of the use made of these Egyptian figures does not prove that my principle is falsely applied. It shows only how absurd idolatry is; and that these figures, once stripped of their primary meaning, led men from one absurdity to another.

The fables of Bellerophon and Perseus follow naturally after that of Pegasus, since he served as a mount for Bellerophon to go and attack the terrifying Chimera; and for Perseus, to fly to the aid of Andromeda, who was exposed to being devoured by a monster.

# THE THEOGONY.

Since *Trofibis* (a) signifies *the poor quality of food*, or a lack of provisions, we can easily see what gave rise to the fable. The colony established in Lycia <note>An ancient region on the southern coast of modern-day Turkey.</note> had as enemies excessive heat, then a harsh cold caused by the proximity of the Taurus Mountains; and finally, poor food and a general state of need. They called the heat *the lion*: this is the zodiac sign that characterizes it. They called winter *the chimera*, or Capricorn; this is again the sign proper to that season. Their third enemy, *Trofibis* or *bad food*, also meaning *the tail of the serpent*, they fashioned from all these pieces a monster composed of a lion's head, a goat's body, and a serpent's tail (b). The fable of Perseus and Andromeda is, likewise, nothing more than a popular way of speaking that has been turned into a fable. It was a common turn of phrase in the Hebrew and Phoenician languages to say that a city or a region was the "daughter" of the rocks, deserts, rivers, or mountains that surrounded it, or which it contained. This is why Jerusalem is often called *the daughter of Zion*; that is to say, *the daughter of dryness, or the daughter of the barren hills* that she contained within her walls. Palestine proper, according to the report of Strabo (b) <note>Strabo (64 BC–24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian whose work is a primary source for ancient geography.</note>, was nothing but a *long maritime coast composed of rocks and a sandy beach*. It was bordered by rocks, or steep cliffs, from Joppa or Jaffa, almost its only port, until
