### The Argonauts.

<margin>* In *Euterpe*, no. 36. <note>The second book of Herodotus’s *Histories* is named after Euterpe, the Muse of Music.</note></margin>
The inhabitants of Colchis <note>An ancient region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Georgia, famous in myth as the destination of the Argonauts.</note> were a very ancient colony of Egypt. Almost all authors assure us of this *(a)*, and one finds proof of it, according to the report of Herodotus \*, in various points of resemblance that were impossible to mistake. They were swarthy and had curly hair like the Egyptians. They had preserved the practice of circumcision, which both groups regarded not as a religious act, but, according to Herodotus's report, as something beneficial to their health. They had apparently adopted this custom among themselves since the time of Joseph <note>The biblical patriarch who became a high-ranking official in Egypt.</note>, when his family was held in high regard due to the still-recent memory of the salvation for which Egypt was indebted to him. The Colchians spoke the same language and had the same customs as the Egyptians; in particular, like them, they applied themselves to working flax <note>The plant used to make linen, which was a major Egyptian export.</note>. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> *(b)* reports the same signs of the origin attributed to them, and he adds

Furthermore, no one is unaware that the Phasis <note>The Rioni River in modern-day Georgia.</note> which flowed through Colchis, carried along gold flakes that people would gather on its banks using sheepskins or shaggy fabrics—as is still practiced today—because the flakes become entangled in the wool and remain there. We need nothing more than these few specifics unique to Colchis to account for the famous fable of the Argonauts <note>In Greek mythology, Jason and the Argonauts traveled to Colchis to retrieve the Golden Fleece; the author suggests the "fleece" was a literal tool for gold mining.</note>.

Since the Colchians followed the same customs as the Egyptians, they undoubtedly announced their common labors through public signs in order to determine their beginning and duration. Their river did not fertilize the countryside as the Nile did in Egypt. When the time suitable for conducting this search had arrived, there was a great interest in not letting this precious material be carried away as far as the sea: it was therefore necessary to disperse at the right moment along the banks of the Phasis, and to hasten to spread sheepskins—still covered in their wool—around the rocks, under the roots of large trees, and in all the inlets of the river, in order to catch the flakes. It was accompanied by the figure of a serpent, the usual symbol of everything that contributed to the subsistence or prosperity of the inhabitants.

The rest of the fable is found in the common idiom of the inhabitants of Colchis <note>An ancient region on the Black Sea coast (modern Georgia), famous in myth for the Golden Fleece.</note>. They likely said that the Golden Fleece and the serpent guarding it were carried away by the arrival of night-watches and regulated sleep. That is to say, the search for gold flakes <note>In Colchis, gold was traditionally harvested by placing sheepskins in rivers to catch drifting gold particles.</note> was neglected when the time came to stay awake well into the night to advance the manufacture of thread and cloth. For this, it was necessary to *regulate sleep* and prescribe its *measure*. It was no longer permitted to sleep whenever one wished. Everyone was subject to a *measure*, to a specific hour, to a *rule*. This *measure of sleep* was then the people's great concern, and they spoke of nothing else. The Greeks, constantly hearing the words *Jason* (*a*), which means *sleep*, and *Mad* or *Mideh*, which means *the rule*; and hearing it said, moreover, that *Jason*, led by *Mideh*, carried away the Golden Fleece; they imagined the voyage of the ship.

### XXXIII.

->*Argus.*<-

Weaving was famous in Athens, on the island of Amorgos (*a*), and in Colchis, as well as in Egypt. However, the season for this manufacture was not the same in these different regions. In Egypt, people were heavily occupied with public works—such as the cleaning of canals, haymaking, harvesting, and the threshing of grain—during the months of February, March, April, and May. ### XXXIV.

->*Circe.*<-

The same Isis, when brought to Italy with her various accompaniments, gave rise to a fable of an entirely different character. Mythologists have believed that she was an emblem of sensual pleasure <term>volupté: intense physical or sensual delight, often implies a lack of moral restraint</term> which reduces men to the condition of beasts. From a very sensible proverb, they have made a pitiful fable.

Little by little, the understanding of these very simple figures and names—which were used in festivals where everything had become an unchanging ceremonial—was lost. The use of <term>cursive writing</term> <note>original: "écriture courante." As the Egyptians moved from hieroglyphs (pictorial signs) to simpler scripts for daily use, the original symbolic meaning of the drawings was forgotten.</note> caused their meaning to be neglected; and furthermore, nothing contributed more to this forgetting than the custom of not calculating the <term>sacred year</term> <note>The Egyptian "vague year" consisted of exactly 365 days, without a leap year, meaning it drifted through the seasons over a 1,461-year cycle.</note> exactly, but rather continually pushing back its beginning by an entire day every four years. According to the order of later times, all these figures did indeed succeed one another in the same fashion, but in seasons and months with which they no longer had any true relationship. Thus Sudec <note>A name often associated in 18th-century scholarship with the Phoenician deity of justice, equated here with Saturn.</note>, or Cronus, or Saturn, became the father of Jupiter and Isis. Saturn, Rhea, Tethys, and Titan were their ancestors: the Titans were regarded as the children of *Ur* or *Uranus*, and of *Ops*. Many genealogists stop there. Others, like Diodorus, <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote extensively on Egyptian mythology.</note> make Uranus and Ops the children of Acmon. The Egyptians, in their genealogy, go back as far as Vulcan. Now, Acmon, the Coppersmith, and Vulcan are one and the same thing.

Because Saturn—or Cronus—was necessarily connected with the perfect equity of judgments rendered without respect of persons <note>To act "without respect of persons" means to judge fairly without being influenced by a person's status or wealth.</note>, by a group of isolated and disinterested judges, it was said that Saturn had reigned with perfect gentleness and integrity. ### XL.

->*Animals honored with religious worship.*<-

The natural effect of this opinion <note>referring to the belief in the transmigration of souls discussed on the previous page</note> was to spare the blood of animals, even though God placed them near us only to serve us and to nourish us. It is true that good reasons were found not to deprive the people of the flesh of the ox, which is an abundant and perfect nourishment. It is true that there was a kind of tacit agreement between the provinces of Egypt <note>The author refers to the various "nomes" or districts of ancient Egypt, which often had different patron deities and sacred animals.</note> to make use, one of the flesh of sheep, the other of the flesh of young goats, so as not to be deprived of a useful trade, and of too much assistance all at once. But the Egyptian priests commonly abstained from eating the flesh of any beast whatsoever: and in general all the animals whose names the stars bear were regarded by the Egyptians with veneration as having been the first retreat of their gods, and potentially being that of the souls of their dead relatives. They no longer looked except with a religious fear upon those in whom they knew, without being able to doubt it, that Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and fertility.</note> and Isis <note>The Egyptian goddess of healing and magic, wife of Osiris.</note> had made their home, such as the ram, the

### XLI.

### *The Origin of Apis and Mnevis.*

By chance, a calf was found in Memphis that had several spots in a shape approaching a circle or a crescent—symbols so deeply respected among them. This singularity, which was actually nothing and deserved no more attention than the white spots seen on the foreheads of horses or elsewhere, they took for the mark of Osiris and Isis, imprinted upon the animal that their gods cherished. A melancholic mind <note>original: "cervelle hypocondre"; in the 18th century, this referred to someone prone to obsessive or superstitious delusions</note> took it into its head to believe, and to persuade others, that this was an apparition of the Governor <note>A reference to Osiris as the divine ruler of Egypt</note>, a visit that the protector of Egypt deigned to pay them. This miraculous calf, after having been preferred for the usual ceremonial, was housed in the finest part of Memphis. Its dwelling became a temple. The Heavens, as a way to represent the year or the succession of the twelve signs [of the zodiac], was no longer understood by the common people. This image was chosen to signify the year because it is composed of twelve months that follow one another without interruption. This is so certainly true that the Greeks gave the name *Lycabas* to the year, which signifies *the march of the wolves*. <note>A poetic Greek term for "year," derived from *lykos* (wolf) and *basis* (step or path).</note>

The ox was undoubtedly the object of a fashionable devotion: but to have it serve as a support for the vat where the ministers of the living God washed themselves was to degrade, through the most humble of all services, the very animal that was worshipped among neighboring peoples. Conversely, Jeroboam, the irreconcilable enemy of Solomon, intended to profit from the people's inclination toward this animal when, upon his return from Egypt, he tried to divert the Israelites from going to Jerusalem by binding them to Dan and Bethel through the erection of the golden calves he placed there. Whence, finally, could the worship that the Hebrews paid in the desert to a cast bull <note>This refers to the "Golden Calf" incident in the Book of Exodus.</note> have come, if not from the vivid impression that the pomp of the festivals of Apis and Mnevis <term>Apis and Mnevis were sacred bulls worshipped in Ancient Egypt as physical incarnations of deities (Ptah/Osiris and Ra, respectively).</term> had made upon their minds since childhood, while they were in the land of Goshen, near Heliopolis and Memphis?

That the ram, the goat, the lamb, and the kid were worshipped in Egypt as well as the bull, we find another proof in the refusal Moses made to use the permission Pharaoh gave him to celebrate the festival of the Lord without leaving Egypt—without going, as many peoples did, to solemnize their festivals upon the mountains.

### XLIV.

->*The secret of the Egyptian mysteries.*<-

When one wishes to learn what it is possible to know of this Egyptian religion, which provokes curiosity through its mysterious display; one does not fail to read greedily Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, the treatise on *Isis and Osiris*, some other works by Plutarch, the writings of Plato, Porphyry, or such other scholars who had traveled to Egypt, and frequently conversed with the priests of Isis, the most mysterious people in the universe. One imagines that it is in such books that one must seek the understanding of symbolic figures, or that it will be found nowhere else. But after having read them, one is astonished to find nothing there but the stories of common people, or stale allegories without connection, without dignity, without utility; or finally, a stilted metaphysics, in the subtleties of which our deists <note>In the 18th century, "deists" were thinkers who sought a natural religion based on reason rather than revelation, often projecting their own complex philosophies onto ancient cultures.</note> love to lose themselves, but of which it is ridiculous to think that simple antiquity could have had the slightest knowledge. Those who were initiated into it bound themselves by oath to communicate nothing to the common people of what had been revealed to them. Let us then see—and this is how we shall conclude our essay on the religion of the Egyptians—let us see what these much-vaunted mysteries were, and let us penetrate, if possible, into these secrets, despite the veils and prohibitions that render them inaccessible.

Originally, there was nothing less mysterious than the religion of the Egyptians. At its start, it was fundamentally the same as that of Job and Jethro in Arabia; that of Melchizedek <note>A king and priest mentioned in the Book of Genesis, often cited by historians of this era as a symbol of "natural" or primitive monotheism.</note> in Canaan; and that of Abimelech in Palestine. In a word, it was the religion of Noah and of the Patriarchs, his children, who founded the first colonies. This religion consisted of worshipping the Most High. Justice and labor were recommended; the dead were treated honorably; a better future was expected. Far from the figures displayed to the eyes of the people hiding any mysteries, they were presented in public only to make them understand...

They first familiarized themselves with these ideas because it was dangerous not to conform to them, and later they became their most zealous defenders. It all happened by degrees. They initially adapted to the common language because they believed they could not withstand the torrent; however, they studied in private whatever they could gather regarding the interpretation of the ancient script. They thus admitted both the popular stories and the explanations that invalidated them; they merely took the precaution of requiring silence from those whom they wished to instruct more thoroughly.

Instruction thus took on a mysterious and important air without destroying any of what the people believed. <margin>THE POETIC HEAVEN.</margin>...of men. In this way, they avoided driving the people into a frenzy. It was already a great injustice on the part of these priests to hold the truth captive and to appropriate it for themselves by excluding others.

Such a criminal disposition could only lead to further decline. Indeed, everything degenerated more and more. The testing of disciples and the oath of inviolable secrecy were practices that made a strong impression, and thus they were maintained with great precision. Ritual <note>original: "le cérémonial," referring to the external rites and formal procedures of a religion</note> is easily maintained in all religions; it is often embellished rather than discarded, because it does not challenge the passions—which it leaves largely undisturbed—and sometimes even flatters them. Truth and instruction did not fare as well as ritual. They became disfigured from age to age, sometimes through the ignorance and superstition of the priests, sometimes through their greed, but above all through their obsession with systematic fantasies <note>original: "rêveries systématiques," referring to the complex, speculative theories the priests invented to explain ancient symbols</note> by which the most clever among them tried to explain the symbolic writing. They were far more satisfied with these inventions than with the few simple and straightforward truths that their predecessors had been content to teach them.

These practices had no relation to the gods, because the gods arrived later; and they are only called "mysteries" <note>The "Mysteries" refers to ancient secret societies and rites, such as those at Eleusis, which promised initiates special knowledge.</note> because it was necessary to find trustworthy people to whom one could explain what all of this signified in ancient times. The objective of this ancient instruction revolved around three points, which were: first, to teach men—who were scattered and hindered by a thousand obstacles—the way to feed and clothe themselves through certain regulations or precautions based on experience; second, to treat one another with gentleness; and third, finally, to live with an equity <term>Equity: In this context, living with moral fairness and justice toward others.</term> that would ensure them a better life after death. The words of Cicero are clear. # OF THE HEAVENS.

<margin>THEOGONY. An explanation of the fable of Ceres.</margin>
Ceres’s journey is a tapestry of short stories invented to give some sense to the terms and figures that were preserved in the festivals without being understood; but which, in their original institution, aimed to represent the upheaval of the earth’s surface caused by the flood <note>The author refers to the Great Deluge, a common historical framework in the 18th century to explain geological and mythological origins.</note>, the changes in the air and the seasons, the loss of ancient abundance, and the long hardships that farming had to overcome. The Isis who appeared in this festival, commemorating the sad state of humanity after the flood, represented the earth; and she was then given a name suited to expressing the change that the flood had introduced into our dwelling place, the exterior of which it had overturned and broken. She was named Ceres, which signifies *ruin, fracture, upheaval* (a). This desolate mother weeps for the loss of her dear daughter. She regrets the lost abundance—that ancient fertility which the waters bursting from beneath the earth had taken from her. She mourns the grain, hidden and confused with a mass of bad plants that choke it, or cast uselessly into sterile fields, or carried away by the winds and by the ravage of great...

<margin>The torches of Ceres.</margin>
Humans were for a long time in distress, devastated by rains and by cold, forced to gather stalks of giant fennel <term>giant fennel: *Ferula communis*, whose dry stalks were used in antiquity as torches because the inner pith burns slowly</term>, or other dry or resinous <note>original OCR: "fineuſes," likely a typo for "résineuses"</note> materials to make torches equally suited to warming them and lighting the long winter nights, which had been unknown until then. From this come the torches that are inseparable from the commemorative signs of this sad state of the human race.

<margin>The poppies of Ceres.</margin>
To survive, they first made use of seeds or oil of sesame, or acorns, pomegranates, and other fruits that were found at random among the thorns and brambles. Little by little, they learned to regularly cultivate certain seeds. The poppy, by its speed in growing and by the multitude of its seeds, was the plant that best suited them in the beginnings, and whose heads we often see in the hand of Ceres.

### THE THEOGONY.

The first harvest, more abundant than before, brought back hope & joy. This is all that *Bobo* (a) means. The plow was invented to speed up *the breaking of the furrows*, which is the meaning of *Triptolemus* (b). Through the help of wood & wicker, which are easily worked for any purpose, they multiplied *the instruments suited to aiding human labor, & to preserving the harvest*. THEOGONY.
</margin>
The primary intention of the ceremony of rural festivals was originally reduced to making the assembled people understand four things that one no longer dared to tell them once they had converted the symbols into so many gods.

**1º.** They were warned to glorify the Supreme Being above all, the unique intelligence who guides the universe at his will.

**2º.** They were informed of the progress of the sun, the specific circumstances of the month, or the order of the year.

**3º.** They were informed of the schedule of the festivals.

**4º.** They were urged to observe the dog days <note>original: "jours caniculaires." These are the hottest days of the year, historically linked to the rising of the "Dog Star" Sirius, which signaled the flooding of the Nile.</note>, and the rising of the waters in Egypt, or other circumstances that concerned farming according to the nature of the country. Nothing was better conceived than this festival in the simplicity of its institution. Cicero very well understood its end and intention, which was to teach men how to subsist, to regulate their labor, to live in peace, and to hope, by honoring God, for a better future. Finally, it is not possible to better express the intention of these festivals, according to the thought of Cicero or according to my explanation, than by giving them the name they bore. In Greece they were called the *Thesmophoria* (a): in Phoenicia, and among the ancient Latins,

These objects of their belief, and the foundation of their practice, were destroyed nowhere, but were disfigured by the addition of an infinity of new ideas and absurd customs.

Spiritual worship, and adoration in spirit and in truth, were converted by greed into a purely carnal religion <note>A religion focused on physical desires or worldly needs rather than spiritual growth.</note> which desires the goods of the earth more than justice. The indifference and crudeness of the people caused them to neglect the understanding of the signs established in ancient times to instruct them. The same ignorance made them convert the signs of the sun, the seasons, and the festivals—where symbolic humans and animals were used—into as many gods with which their imagination populated the heavens. A new mistake caused these supposed celestial men or women to be taken for persons once distinguished on earth, and transported into the stars after their death. The abuse of language and of figurative animals introduced the veneration of real animals, the persuasion of metempsychosis <term>metempsychosis: the transmigration of the soul, especially its reincarnation after death into a new body of the same or a different species.</term>, and a life entirely full of superstitious practices.

The religion of the Egyptians and all the paganism that arose from it are nothing but the religion of the patriarchs, corrupted by extravagant additions. It is enough to cast an eye upon that barker <note>original: "aboyeur"—a reference to the dog-headed god Anubis, whom the author interprets here as a mere herald or sign.</note> who has a dog’s head on his shoulders and wings on his feet, to sense that this figure was a warning to think of departure <note>The author suggests these figures were originally practical signs, perhaps indicating the need to move livestock or people before a seasonal flood.</note>. At the mere sight of a lion’s body joined to the head of a young girl, one perceives that this arrangement refers to the sun’s passage through the signs of Leo and Virgo. One can easily judge the purpose of the other figures by these examples. They all served...

<summary>The author argues that ancient Egyptian symbols were originally simple seasonal and agricultural signs that were later over-complicated by philosophers. He suggests that complex mythological figures, like the Sphinx or Anubis, were once practical reminders of the sun's position or the need for seasonal migration.</summary>

<page-num>398</page-num>
<header>HISTORY</header>

<margin>
THE POETIC HEAVENS.
</margin>
...clearly markers and characters. How then did they become gods, if not because these figures were converted by the ignorance and greed of the people into so many real objects, into so many powers conforming to their inclinations? This produced an insane cult and a prodigious mass of fables, followed by philosophical systems as laughable as the fables themselves. With the exception of a few regular assemblies where public authority maintained some vestiges of truth alongside ancient customs, everything degenerated more and more through the freedom of embellishments and interpretations. Gods multiplied in the mouths of the people just as the symbols did, and even in proportion to the different names given to the same symbol. Often the smallest ambiguities <note>original: "équivoques"</note> arising from differences in pronunciation, often the diversity of garments the figure wore, often a simple change of location—the slightest addition or subtraction—formed a new god. We have seen how many different forms Isis <note>The Egyptian goddess, whom the author believes was originally a symbol of the earth or the public calendar.</note> took, under which she was at first difficult to recognize. Molech <note>original: "Moloc"</note>, Baal, Marnas, Adonis, Attis <note>original: "Atys"</note>, Ammon, and Jupiter are all nothing but the same Osiris <note>The Egyptian god, here interpreted as a singular original symbol that was renamed and reinvented by different cultures.</note>.

<summary>The author explains how simple symbolic markers evolved into a complex and "insane" pagan mythology through popular ignorance, linguistic shifts, and varied artistic interpretations. He argues that many famous gods from different cultures are actually just variations of the same original Egyptian symbol, Osiris.</summary>

<page-num>399</page-num>
<header>OF THE HEAVENS.</header>
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<margin>
THEOGONY.
<note>The branch of mythology that deals with the origin and genealogy of the gods.</note>
</margin>
Thoth, Anubis, Hermes, Camillus, Daedalus, Icarus, Mercury, Aesculapius, and Janus are nothing more than the Dog Star <note>original: "la canicule." The author identifies these various figures as personifications of the star Sirius, which warned of the Nile's rising.</note> in disguise. Menes, Minos, Menophis, Mnevis, Memnon, Apollo, Mars, Dionysus, Bacchus, Proteus, and Hercules are nothing but Horus <note>The Egyptian sky god, whom the author views here as a primary symbol for the sun or the seasons that was renamed by later civilizations.</note> in various forms. Two symbols were often confused with one another. The lyre, of which Mercury is considered the inventor, is also found in the hands of Apollo; furthermore, the serpent, which is inseparable from Aesculapius, is also placed alongside Apollo. This occurred because the symbols for the Dog Star and for plowing <note>referring to agricultural cycles</note> had an essential connection to the celebration of festivals and the very survival of society. Conversely, the same symbol often gave rise to several new deities by changing its name and attributes, or by moving from one province to another. This is how the Aesculapius of Epidaurus has a very different function from the Marcol <note>A reference to Markolis, a deity of the Canaanites often associated with Mercury or the Greek Hermes.</note> of the Canaanites, even though they were both originally nothing but Thoth—the warning of the star <note>Thoth was associated with the star Sirius; the author sees the "warning" of the star's appearance as the root of the character.</note> that brought safety and wealth to the Egyptians.

With this multiplicity of protectors, there was much to choose from and enough to satisfy every taste. Every district had its tutelary <note>protective or guardian</note> gods, whose histories were told and whose monuments were displayed. These were the gods of the country, friendly gods, and regarding the...

<summary>The author argues that a wide variety of Greek, Roman, and Canaanite gods are merely renamed versions of Egyptian symbols, specifically the Dog Star (Sirius) and Horus. He explains that these deities multiplied as symbols were moved between regions or given new attributes by different cultures.</summary>

<margin>
THE POETIC HEAVENS.

...on whom one could count. It was only natural to give them the place of honor. But this preference did not go so far as to close the door to foreign gods. They did not wish to fall out with any of these powers. They were admitted into one another's company; and often, gods hatched or derived from the same symbol <note>The author argues that many distinct gods actually share a single origin in Egyptian agricultural or astronomical signage.</note> found themselves together with an array of attributes and functions that led people to believe they originated from very different families and regions. Sometimes, quarrels over precedence <note>original: "le pas," referring to the order of importance in formal processions or social standing.</note> arose between them. Their nobility was certainly very difficult to untangle, since it was—much like that of many of our earthly divinities—entirely imaginary. The Greek chroniclers took care to create genealogies for them: they managed this as best they could. The celestial court in Egypt was not the same as in Greece. In Egypt, it was Osiris who lit the world: in Greece, Osiris or Jupiter was relieved of this duty; he was left with the scepter and the thunderbolt. But the chariot of the day was given to Horus or Apollo. Jupiter could not do everything nor be everywhere. Thus, he was given lieutenants with separate districts. Everything took shape: the functions and histories of the gods were arranged: and by attributing to them whatever each...

<summary>This page describes how the Greeks adapted Egyptian symbols into a complex pantheon, creating imaginary genealogies and dividing divine responsibilities—such as separating the sun's light from the supreme rule—among different deities like Jupiter and Apollo.</summary>

<header>OF THE HEAVENS.</header>

<margin>THEOGONY. <note>Theogony refers to the branch of mythology that deals with the origins and genealogies of the gods.</note></margin>
...each nation published it in its own way; by adding to it the adventures of the ministers of the temples, and those of the kings who had favored their worship; but above all by excusing the misconduct of women through the alleged disguises of these gods enamored of their beauty, they formed this heap of mythology, in which it is not surprising that one finds neither sense, nor connection, nor order of place or time, nor any regard for reason or for morals. However senseless most of these fabulous tales may be, since they formed part of the strange theology of our fathers <note>The author uses "our fathers" to refer to the ancient civilizations, particularly the Greeks and Romans, whose culture formed the basis of European education.</note>, people have at all times tried to discover their true origin. I have ventured my own conjectures on the same subject, because they seemed to me to approach certainty, and because the whole could be developed with as much propriety as profit. As for the minor details of these follies, the same does not apply. Assuredly, there is no subject where it is more permissible to limit one's knowledge <note>The author suggests that while the origins of these myths are worth studying, the absurd details of every specific fable are not worth the effort of a scholar.</note>.

<summary>The author explains how mythology became a confused collection of stories used to justify human scandals and glorify kings, asserting that while their origins are worth investigating, the absurd details are not.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as an explanation of the frontispiece (the decorative illustration facing the title page) for the work. It follows the index of the first volume and sets the philosophical tone for the entire series, emphasizing practical utility over abstract metaphysical speculation.</meta>

# EXPLANATION

## OF THE FRONTISPIECE.

IT represents Democritus <note>Democritus (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was a Greek philosopher known for his "atomic" theory—the idea that the universe is made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note> who has retired into the tombs of Abdera <note>An ancient city in Thrace, the birthplace of Democritus. The philosopher was said to frequent cemeteries to contemplate the nature of life and death.</note> his homeland, and who renounces the occupations of society, to meditate, without distraction, on the structure of the world which he believes was formed by the settlement and by the meeting of small pre-existing pieces which he likes to call Atoms. A Citizen comes to place near the Philosopher a slate on which he has written this verse:

->Man is not meant to build the earth, but to cultivate it.<- <note>original Greek: "οὐ μὲν δημιουργεῖν ἀνθρώπινον, ἀλλὰ γεωργεῖν."</note>

> *Man is not at all made to construct the earth, but to cultivate it.*

The laborers and the passersby, who read or who hear this epigram read, mock the Philosopher. One shrugs his shoulders: another bursts out laughing: all feel that we have received enough intelligence to regulate our work and our morals; but that we can understand nothing in that which has not been entrusted to our care. This is the conclusion of this entire work. <note>This reflects a common 18th-century view that humans should focus on observable nature and practical science rather than "useless" theories about how the universe was physically constructed.</note>

*The Names and the order of the Plates are found at the end of Volume II.*

---

->From the Printing Press of JACQUES VINCENT.<- <note>Jacques Vincent was a prominent printer in Paris during the mid-18th century.</note>

It establishes the book's theme: that human intelligence is best suited for practical work and morality rather than speculative cosmology.</summary>

<meta>This page explains the symbolic frontispiece of the work, setting a tone of practical humility over abstract speculation. # EXPLANATION
## OF THE FRONTISPIECE.

It represents **Democritus** <note>Democritus (c. 460 – 370 BC) was a Greek philosopher from Abdera, famous for proposing that the world is made of indivisible particles.</note> who has retired to the tombs of **Abdera**, his homeland, and who renounces the occupations of society to meditate, without distraction, upon the structure of the world. He believes this world was formed by the settling and the gathering of tiny pre-existing pieces that he chooses to call **Atoms** <note>The term "atom" comes from the Greek *atomos*, meaning "indivisible."</note>. A citizen comes to place beside the **Philosopher** a slate upon which he has written this verse:

->It is not for man to create, but rather to cultivate.<-
<note>Original Greek: οὐ μὲν δημιουργεῖν ἀνθρώπινον, ἀλλὰ γεωργεῖν.</note>

->*Man is not at all made to build the earth, but to cultivate it.*<-

The laborers and passersby, who read or hear this epigram read aloud, mock the Philosopher. One shrugs his shoulders; another bursts into laughter. All feel that we have received enough intelligence to regulate our work and our morals, but that we can understand nothing of that which has not been entrusted to our care. This is the conclusion of this entire work.

->*The Names and the order of the Plates are found*<-
->*at the end of Volume II.*<-
